title: What happened at Kent State?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the May 4, 1970 Kent State shootings, in which Ohio National Guardsmen fired on Vietnam War protesters on the Kent State University campus, killing four students and wounding nine. They cover the lead-up from the Vietnam War and Nixon's April 1970 invasion of Cambodia, the escalating protests and rioting in Kent (Friday and Saturday, including the burning of the ROTC building), Governor James Rhodes' press conference, the martial law confusion, the Monday confrontation on Blanket Hill, the aftermath (official reports, FBI findings, the 1979 civil settlement, the regret-style statement, the university's memorial efforts), and later theories including a possible earlier shot. They also cover the Jackson State shootings ten days later in Mississippi, where two Black students were killed. The episode closes with a listener letter from a former prison guard about prison guards' portrayal, and a sponsor read for Lynda.com.

segments.title: Opening banter and Neil Young's Ohio
segments.summary: Hosts open with snow talk and chat about Neil Young's song Ohio, then introduce the Kent State shootings as a major event in American history.

segments.title: Background: Vietnam, Nixon and the Cambodia invasion
segments.summary: The hosts trace the Vietnam background from French withdrawal in the 1950s through American involvement, Nixon's Vietnamization promise, and his April 30, 1970 announcement of the invasion of Cambodia, which sparked protests.

segments.title: Kent State before the shootings and the May 1 protest
segments.summary: The hosts describe Kent State's character compared with Ohio State and a May 1 campus anti-war protest, after which students burned a constitution symbolically and went drinking.

segments.title: Friday and Saturday riots and the National Guard arrival
segments.summary: Friday night bonfires, bottle throwing and window breaking led Mayor Leroy Satrom to call Governor James Rhodes and close the bars. On Saturday protesters burned the ROTC building and cut hoses, and the National Guard arrived.

segments.title: Sunday press conference and martial law confusion
segments.summary: On Sunday Governor Rhodes called protesters the worst type of people America harbors and compared them to Mussolini's brown shirts, and mentioned possibly declaring martial law. Guardsmen took control of campus believing martial law was in effect, while the university distributed flyers banning assemblies.

segments.title: Monday confrontation and the shootings on Blanket Hill
segments.summary: On Monday, May 4, thousands gathered on the Commons. General Canterbury's bullhorn order to disperse was met with rocks, guardsmen pushed protesters down the hill, were cornered by a fence, turned at the top of Blanket Hill and fired about 61 to 67 shots in roughly thirteen seconds, killing four students and wounding nine. Faculty marshal Glenn Frank helped calm the crowd.
topics: Allison Krause Jeffrey Miller Sandra Scheuer William Schroeder

segments.title: Aftermath, investigations, settlement and apology question
segments.summary: Nixon's and Agnew's reactions, the claim that guardsmen planned to fire, the self-defense claim, the Presidential Commission and FBI findings, the failed federal trial, the 1979 civil settlement of $675,000, and the regretful statement that was not an apology. The university's memorial efforts and the visitors center are also covered.

segments.title: Later theories: Oliver Stone, the audio recording and Terry Norman
segments.summary: The hosts discuss theories about snipers and government agitators, a recording with commands like get set and fire, and a claim that a photographer, Terry Norman, may have fired an earlier shot.

segments.title: Jackson State shootings
segments.summary: Ten days later at Jackson State University in Mississippi, police fired into a dormitory after a building fire and protests, killing two Black students, Philip Gibbs and James Green. Hosts note how little attention it receives.

segments.title: Listener mail on prison guards
segments.summary: A former death row guard writes that the hosts' tone toward prison guards in the capital punishment episode was unfair, explaining inmates have razor access rights and guards have feelings. The hosts discuss the portrayal of guards in media such as Oz.

segments.title: Outro and sponsor read
segments.summary: The hosts suggest further reading on Kent State and Jackson State, invite listener contact, and close with a Lynda.com sponsor read.
